That’s the gorgeously perverse opening of “Dead Outlaw,” the feel-good musical of the season, if death and deadpan feel good to you.

That Dead Outlaw so neatly reflects the zeitgeist as it transfers uptown is representative of the way David Yazbek, Erik Della Penna, and Itamar Moses’s deceptively small-scale musical follows the stream of the hyperspecific into deep and vast currents in the American psyche.
If you choose the one with the corpse, know that this weird show is very much alive.
Both are rousing testaments to the ingenuity of their creators, who turn dying into high art.

David Yazbek ’s latest curio, which opened April 27 at the Longacre Theatre, is a waggish, walloping, what-in-tarnation musical; the sort of coup that is so sublimely strange and strangely profound, it will revive your faith in Broadway itself.
For all its irreverence and comedy, Cromer and his team have ensured that we see Elmer’s posthumous life for what it really was: twisted and maddening in its lack of ethics.
On Sunday, it reopened uptown at the Longacre Theatre, where it’s now the weirdest, funniest and saddest show on Broadway.
Deadpan humor gets no deader than Durand’s performance.
I was wildly charmed by this chronicle of this corpse’s adventures, as directed by David Cromer.
Eccentric, silly, and moving, the tale of Elmer McCurdy is one that truly needs to be seen to be believed.
Dead Outlaw...is entertainment for a paying audience, after all.
An extreme story told, acted, and sung brilliantly in Dead Outlaw.
Nonetheless, even as the final note is played, it’s a little hard to know why the show’s creators, including the talented book writer Itamar Moses, felt this mostly true-life story was so compelling.
But this self-conscious slice of Americana winds up almost as creepy as clever, and less resonant than it might intend.
As the best new musical of the season, Dead Outlaw proves that producers don’t need a well-known IP or $31 million to make an impact.
Dead Outlaw unearths the corpse of forgotten history — elevating a twisty little yarn into a bizarro-world elegy to how the American Dream can curdle into violence, cruelty, and casual indifference.
And it is, by far, the best, most sublime musical of the season.
Rounded out by the indisputable acting talent, it is wildly creative, wickedly funny, and definitely worth the ride.

cn.t: Critics praise this darkly comic musical about a mummified outlaw as bold, original, and wildly entertaining, with an excellent genre-hopping score. The offbeat true story and sardonic sensibility won't appeal to traditional Broadway crowds.

sg.ra: Longacre's proscenium is narrow (35ft wide, 34'10" high) and the house is shallow, so Row D sits very close without neck-craning; Center Orchestra rows D-L fall inside the mezzanine overhang line (which starts around Row H) but the overhang is shallow enough that top-of-stage cut-off is not reported here, unlike deeper houses.

Longacre is a small-to-mid house (1,077 seats) so 'rear' orchestra is still close by Broadway standards; rows L-N sit behind the mezzanine overhang line (starts ~H) which trims a small slice of upper stage but preserves intimacy and drops the price noticeably versus premium D-K.

Longacre's mezzanine is 'not too high' per SeatPlan - the overhang from the balcony only starts at Row B, so Row A gets a clean head-on elevated view, and unusually generous front-row legroom is a Longacre-specific quirk called out on BroadwayWorld.

Rows D-E sit under the balcony overhang (starts Row B) but Longacre's balcony is small (249 seats, 7 rows) so the overhang depth is modest; sources consistently flag D-E as the honest middle-ground for elevated sightlines before rows F-J start feeling far from the stage.

Longacre's mezzanine rake flattens toward the back per SeatPlan ('the rake may also be slightly too shallow if a taller patron is sitting in front'), and rows F-J are explicitly called out as 'problematic' and 'not the best on account of their considerable distance from the stage' - the small house becomes a disadvantage here since the balcony takes over the better upper-level views.

Longacre-specific quirk: the front balcony rail sits high enough that multiple TripAdvisor reviewers at 5'5" and 5'7" had to lean over the bar the whole show (Macbeth 2022, Swept Away-era 2025), so Row B beats Row A for most patrons - the opposite of the usual 'front row is always best' advice. Also avoid the four structural pillars between rows B and C on the center aisles.

sg.ra: Longacre's balcony is the oldest-school part of the house - a 1913 Henry B. Herts design with four structural pillars between B-C and a steep rake that gets sound-dead at the back; SeatPlan explicitly warns 'sound quality may be inferior toward the rear' and rows D-G compound distance + pillar risk + tight legroom.
